title: Surface-tuning nanoporous AuCu3 engineering syngas proportion by electrochemical conversion of CO2
abstract: The direct electrochemical conversion of CO2 to syngas with controllable composition remains challenging. In this work, driven by concentration gradient, a simple air-heating aided strategy has been developed to adjust surface composition of the self-supporting nanoporous AuCu3 alloy. According to Fick First Law, the interior Cu atoms of the AuCu3 alloy with Au-rich surface gradually segregated outwards during heating, realizing Cu-rich surface eventually. Correspondingly, the competing electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (ECR) to CO and hydrogen evolution reactions (HER) were tactfully balanced on these alloy surfaces, thus achieving proportion-tunable syngas (CO/H2). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations on the Gibbs free energy change of the COOH* and H* (ΔGCOOH*, ΔGH*) on the alloy surfaces were conducted, which are generally considered as the selectivity descriptors for CO and H2 products, respectively. It shows ΔGCOOH* gradually increases in contrast to the decreased ΔGH* with more Cu on the surface, suggesting H2 is more favored over Cu sites, which is consistent with the declining CO/H2 ratio observed in the experiments. This study reveals that the surface composition controls ECR activity of nanoporous AuCu3 alloy, providing an alternative way to the syngas production with desirable proportion.

sections.text: KEYWORDS AuCu3, surface segregation, CO2 reduction, syngas

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
The catalytic activity and selectivity of nanomaterials are deeply dependent on their surface structure and composition [1–3]. With the development of synthetic chemistry, tremendous advances have been made in improving the catalytic performances, such as preparing porous structures for mass transfer, constructing various alloying structures (solid solution, intermetallic compound, and core–shell structure) and surface segregation structures, exposing specific facets as well as surface modification [4–10]. Especially, the catalysts with threedimensional (3D) interconnected porous network, large specific surface area, high conductivity, and flexible composition are favored as the free-standing electrodes in the field of electrochemical energy conversion and storage [11, 12]. Up to now, the structural regulation of porous catalysts focuses on the geometric structure and chemical composition [13–15]. It is found that cyclic voltammetry tests can change the surface composition evolution of nanoporous Pt-Pd@Au core–shell structure from Pt-Pd alloy to ternary Pt-Pd-Au alloy, leading to high activity towards oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) [16]. Snyder et al. synthesized nanoporous PdX (X = Ag, Cu, Ni, Co) alloys and investigated the composition effect on CO adsorption [17]. Chen et al. utilized the surfactant to optimize the dealloying parameters, obtaining the specific facets exposed the porous catalyst for methanol oxide reaction (MOR) and
ORR [18]. These progresses provide deep insights into the structure-performance of nanoporous metals, showing great significance in broad reactions with industrial importance.
Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (ECR) is considered as a promising way to produce valuable chemicals such as CO, CH4, HCOOH, and C2+ products, where how to improve the product selectivity of the catalysts is interesting and challenging [19, 20]. For example, syngas, a mixture with different CO/H2 proportions, can be synthesized by tailoring competing ECR and hydrogen evolution reactions (HER), and further converted to long-chain hydrocarbons by Fisher–Tropsch chemistry. Previously reported nanoporous metals have exhibited excellent performances in ECR due to the exposure of highly active internal surface nanopores, and monolithic self-supported structure [21–23]. It is found that Cu is very active to produce various products [24]. While Ag and Au exhibit high activity and selectivity towards CO [25, 26]. Therefore, constructing nanoporous bimetallic alloys should facilitate to improve their catalytic selectivity to value-added chemicals by synergistic effect. Moreover, the tunable surface composition of the constituted components can further optimize the active sites and product distribution, offering the chance to reveal composition-ECR selectivity relationship [27–30].
Herein, we prepared three typical nanoporous AuCu3 alloy catalysts with different surface Au/Cu ratios (Au-rich, Cu-rich,

The samples can be directly used as 3D self-supporting electrodes, exhibiting surface compositiondependent product distribution, leading to tunable CO/H2 ratios in a wide range by balancing ECR and HER. This result is probably attributed to the effect of surface electronic structures on the adsorption of COOH* and H*, as proved by densily functional theory (DFT) calculations. This work provides a facile strategy to tune syngas composition by using a monolithic electrode, pushing forward the effective utilization of CO2.

sections.heading: 2.1 Preparation of catalysts
sections.text: The preparation of nanoporous AuCu3 with Au-enriched surface was modified following our previous report [32]. Then nanoporous AuCu3 was heated to 100–300 °C at a rate of 5 °C·min−1 and held at that temperature for 8 h in air. The obtained samples were assigned as AuCu3-100, AuCu3-200, and AuCu3-300, respectively.

sections.heading: 2.2 Characterizations
sections.text: X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were collected on a Rigaku Corporation UItima IV diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (40 kV, 40 mA, λ = 1.5418Å). The morphologies and microstructures of the catalysts were investigated by scanning electron microscope (SEM) (ZEISS MERLIN Compact, Germany), transmission electron mecroscope (TEM), (Tecnai G2 Spirit TWIN, FEI), and high resolution TEM (HRTEM) (FEG Talos F200 X, FEI). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were performed on an ESCALAB 250 Xi system, with a monochromatic Al Kα source and photon energy of 1,486.6 eV.

sections.heading: 2.3 Performance evaluation of ECR
sections.text:
Electrochemical measurements were carried out on a CHI760E electrochemical workstation in two-compartment electrochemical cell with standard three-electrode system. The as-treated nanoporous AuCu3 can be directly used as the working electrode, Pt as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl as reference electrode (3.0 M KCl), respectively. The electrolyte solution (0.1 M KHCO3) was purged with high-purity CO2 at a rate of 10 sccm for at least 30 min until it was saturated to pH value of 6.8. And during the reaction, the CO2 was continuously flowed. The applied potentials for ECR activity were compensated and converted versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) according to the equation of E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 V + (0.059 pH). The applied potentials for ECR activity were compensated and converted versus the RHE according to the equation of E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 V + (0.059 pH). The CO2 gas was bubbled into the cathodic compartment at an average rate of 10 sccm (at room temperature and ambient pressure), which was vented directly into the gas sampling loop of a gas chromatograph (GC9790II, Zhejiang Fuli Analyzing Instruments Co. Ltd.). The GC was initiated every 25 min, and high purity nitrogen (99.999%) was used as carrier gas. The separated gas mixtures were passed through a thermal conductivity detector (TCD), where the concentration of hydrogen was analyzed. The concentration of CO was analyzed by a flame ionization detector (FID) with a methanizer. The partial current density of products (iH2 or iCO) and corresponding Faradaic efficiency (F.E. sections.heading: 2.4 Computational method
sections.text:
All the calculations presented in this work were performed using the Vienna ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) code [33, 34]. The exchange-correlation function was described using the generalized gradient approximation (GGA)-Perdew, Burke and Ernzerh of (PBE) function [35]. The electron wave function was expanded using plane waves with an energy cutoff of 400 eV. Energies and forces were converged to be within 10–5 eV and 0.02 eV·Å−1, respectively. Vibrational analysis for all adsorbents has also been carried out, and the thermal corrections to Gibbs free energy for all adsorbents were achieved using VASPKIT program.
The experimental results show that the surface composition of AuCu3 catalyst changes obviously after being heated at different temperatures. Due to different mobility rates of Au and Cu atoms, heating the sample results in a variation of the atomic ratio of Au and Cu on the surface. With the increase of temperature, the proportion of Cu and its oxidation state on the surface of the catalyst increases correspondingly. According to this, three model catalysts have been constructed and shown in Fig. S15 in the Electronic Supplementary Material (ESM). AuCu3-100 is modeled using a five-layer slab with a (3×3) unit cell of Au (111) surface (Au:Cu = 2:1, top-layer Cu:O is set to be 6:1), AuCu3-200 is modeled using a five-layer slab with a (3×3) unit cell of Cu(111) surface (Au:Cu = 1:8, top-layer Cu:O is set to be 4:1), AuCu3-300 is modeled with a five-layer slab with a (3×3) unit cell of Cu(111) surface (Au:Cu = 1:22, top-layer Cu:O is set to be 3:1). In all the cases, the vacuum region is set to be 20 Å between repeated slabs, the bottom two layers of the catalysts were fixed at their bulk positions and other layers together with the adsorbents are allowed to relax. The Brillouin zone was sampled by a Γ-centered k-point mesh generated through the Monkhorst-Pack method, 3×3×1 for all the catalysts.

sections.heading: 3 Results and discussion
sections.text:
Original nanoporous AuCu3 was synthesized by oxidative etching of Au20Cu80 according to our previous work, possessing Au-enriched surface [32]. Figure 1 illustrated the surfaceregulation process of nanoporous AuCu3 alloy. The as-prepared

nanoporous AuCu3 alloy with different surface Au/Cu ratios was obtained by air-heating treatment from 100 to 300 °C. Then, a series of characterizations and electrochemical tests were performed to analyze the structures of AuCu3 alloy and explore their surface composition-ECR selectivity relationship.
As shown in Fig. 2(a), XRD patterns of all the samples well match that of AuCu3 alloy, where the diffraction peaks at 41.68°, 48.52°, 71.05°, and 85.89° can be assigned to the (111), (200), (220), and (311) planes of the fcc AuCu3, respectively (JCPDS No. 35-1357). However, several weak diffraction peaks that correspond to fcc Au (JCPDS No. 04-0784) can be observed on the original AuCu3. The new rising diffraction peaks are for the CuO resulted from inevitable oxidation of surface Cu atoms (Fig. S1 in the ESM). The result demonstrates that Au atoms diffused inwards and formed AuCu3 alloy, while surface segregated Cu atoms were partially oxidized. Besides, the color changes of AuCu3 alloy were visibly observed from brown to brick-red and finally to black during air-heating process, further confirming the interdiffusion of surface Au and interior Cu atoms (Fig. S2 in the ESM).
The SEM images in Fig. 2(b) and Figs. S3–S5 in the ESM show 3D continuous nanoporous structure with a ligament for all samples. SEM-energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) analyses (Fig. S6 and Table S1 in the ESM) show that the surface proportion of Cu gradually increases from AuCu3 to AuCu3-300. When compared with the Au/Cu ratio of the whole sample (1:3), the surface segregation of Cu can be deduced. In addition, the average pore size significantly decreases and the surface becomes rougher at elevated temperature (Figs. S3 and S4 in the ESM and Fig. 2(b)). Up to 300 °C, most pores on the surface of AuCu3 alloy have been blocked, which is probably attributed to the oxidation of surface Cu and thus the sintering of Cu2O or CuO species (Figs. S1 and S5 in the ESM). TEM image of AuCu3-200 in Fig. 2(c) displays that most ligaments are masculine, feminine, and saddle-like curvature, which is different from ordinary nanoparticles with relatively definite shape and only convex surface curvature at the corners [36]. As can be seen from HRTEM images of Figs. 2(d)–2(g), lattice fringe spacing of 0.212, 0.229, and 0.206 nm, corresponds to Au (111), AuCu3
(111), and Cu2O (111), respectively. Compared with previously reported AuCu3 alloy with Au-rich surface, the appearance of Cu2O lattice indicates that heating drives the migration of Cu from the interior to the surface, and accelerates the oxidation of surface Cu atoms exposed in air [37, 38]. EDS elemental mappings (Figs.2(h)–2(k)) illustrate that Au and Cu atoms are distributed throughout the entire ligaments.
XPS was used to identify the surface composition and chemical state of nanoporous AuCu3 alloy. The characteristic peaks of Au and Cu can be observed from the XPS full survey spectrum (Fig. S7 in the ESM). Figure 3(a) presents the surface Au/Cu atom ratios of 64:36, 12:88, and 4:96 over AuCu3-100, AuCu3-200, and AuCu3-300, respectively. When X-ray went deeper, similar trend was also observed (Fig. 3(b)). The results prove that the surface Au/Cu ratio can be effectively regulated by temperature-induced element segregation. High resolution Au 4f in pristine nanoporous AuCu3 levels can be split into two spin-orbit pairs at 84.2 and 87.9 eV, attributed to the Au 4f7/2 and 4f5/2, respectively [39]. The positions of Au 4f7/2 and 4f5/2 of the heated AuCu3 shifted to a lower binding energy direction compared to that of the original sample (Fig. 3(c)). On the contrary, the main peaks of Cu 2p move to higher binding energy level (Fig. 3(d)). The electronic interaction between Au and Cu should originate from valence electron redistribution during interdiffusion process, where Cu donates electrons to Au atoms [40]. Furthermore, as the temperature rises, the peak area of copper oxide gets large and satellite peaks appear, suggesting the formation of copper oxides on the surface, in accordance to Cu2O and CuO observed in HRTEM and XRD characterizations [41].
According to the consistent results of SEM, XRD, and XPS, nanoporous AuCu3 catalysts with various surface Au/Cu atomic ratios were obtained, confirming the Cu segregation from interior to surface. Considering that the Cu atom concentration gradually goes down from the inside to outside for the initial AuCu3 alloy, the driving force for the interdiffusion of Au and Cu atoms is more likely to be related to the atom concentration gradient following the Fick First Law. Meanwhile, heating accelerates the atom migration.

The as-obtained self-supported porous alloys were directly used as working electrodes for ECR. Figure S9 in the ESM shows a typical linear sweep volt-amperage (LSV) of the samples. The current density of all the samples is basically the same, indicating that the temperature has no significant influence on the activity of the catalysts. Afterwards the stepped-potential tests were conducted from –0.5 to 1.0 V (vs. RHE). According to Fig. S10 and Eq. (S1) in the ESM, the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) values are determined to be 102.5 cm−2 for AuCu3-100 and 82.5 cm−2 for AuCu3-200, and 52.5 cm−2 for AuCu3-300, respectively. ECSA shows a decreasing trend due to the inevitable sintering with the increase of temperature. Among all the applied potentials, the main reaction products are CO and H2 with total Faraday efficiency of 100%. In order to demonstrate the catalytic activity of porous AuCu3 alloys, the partial current density and partial FE of CO and H2 were further done. For the original nanoporous AuCu3 with Auenriched surface, it shows CO FE of 80%–90% from –0.5 to 1.1 V, and CO dominates the product (Fig. S11 in the ESM). For AuCu3-100, the partial current density of CO increased with the applied potential, while the partial current density of H2 remains unchanged (Figs. 4(a) and 4(b)). The CO/H2 ratio gradually increases from 1:5 to 6:1 (Fig. 4(c)), and CO FE
reaches 95% at –1.1 V (Fig. 4(d)). Therefore, AuCu3-100 still has a higher selectivity towards CO at relatively high potential. In comparison to AuCu3, the increased Cu atoms on the surface mainly contribute to hydrogen evolution and thus affect the CO/H2 ratio. In other words, the Au sites are responsible for the CO production, and Cu sites for the H2 in our AuCu3 system [42]. The CO/H2 ratio is not only determined by the surface Au/Cu ratio but also dependent on the applied potential. When further heated at 200 °C, the surface of nanoporous AuCu3 has been changed into a Cu enriched and partially oxidized. With the potential rising, the CO current density increased first and then decreased (Fig. 4(a)), while the current density of H2 constantly increased (Fig. 4(b)). Under the potential of –0.5 – 1.0 V, the CO FE fluctuates between 44% and 64% (Fig. 4(e)), and the CO/H2 ratio is in a range of 0.5–1.2 (Fig. 4(d)), which can be directly used for methanol synthesis in Fischer–Tropsch process. For AuCu3-300, HER dominates the reaction (Fig. 4(f)), only the mixture of CO/H2 of 1:7 can be obtained. This may be due to the too many Cu atoms located on the surface, and little Au reserved. The increased oxidation state of Cu also hampers the CO selectivity [43]. On the other hand, the nanopores disappear (Fig. S5 in the ESM), and aggregated particles cover the active sites and decrease active area. The results show that the surface Au/Cu ratio determines the selectivity of ECR products, leading to the syngas with different proportions [44]. Furthermore, this work can achieve a wide range of syngas regulation in comparison with the reported similar electrocatalysts (Table S2 in the ESM). In addition, the stability of typical AuCu3-200 sample in the processing CO2 into syngas was studied. At potential of –1.0 V (vs. RHE), after reacting 10 h (Fig. S12 in the ESM), the attenuation of current density was negligible, and the FE of CO and H2 remains unchanged, indicating its good stability. Figures S13 and S14 in the ESM also show that nanoporous structure and crystal phase maintain well after electrolysis.
In order to give deep insights into understanding the relationship of surface composition-ECR performance, DFT was conducted to calculate ΔGCOOH* and ΔGH* [45, 46], because the conversion from CO2 to COOH* is the decisive step for CO formation in the whole ECR process; while the formation of H* is the rate-limiting step for HER. According to the results of XPS, Au2Cu, AuCu8, and AuCu22 models with several oxygen atoms on the surface were constructed to represent AuCu3-100, AuCu3-200, and AuCu3-300 alloy surfaces in Fig. S15 in the ESM. The results (Fig. 5) indicate that conversion

reactions from CO2 to COOH* and H* to H2 are exothermic, suggesting that the two steps are easily to occur, in accordance with previously reported results [47]. The ΔGCOOH* increases from Au2Cu to AuCu22 in contrast to decreasing ΔGH*, demonstrating that Cu favors HER over ECR to CO. This result well agrees with the trend of product selectivity obtained from AuCu3-100 to AuCu3-300. It is generally acknowledged that Cu has a lower hydrogen binding energy than Au. When the surface is converted to Cu-rich structure, it can significantly promote the formation of H*. Therefore, it is inferred that surface Cu segregation and oxidation contribute to HER, which block the exposure of Au sites and thus lead to lower CO FE and various syngas proportions.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusions
sections.text: In summary, nanoporous AuCu3 alloy with tunable surface Au/Cu ratios was obtained by a simple air-heating strategy, where the concentration gradient provides the driving force for atom segregation and heating accelerates the diffusion rate of Cu atoms. The nanoporous AuCu3 alloy catalysts exhibited surface composition-dependent ECR performance, where more Cu atoms segregated to surface, the more H2 was formed, which was more likely to be attributed to increasing ΔGCOOH* and decreasing ΔGH*. Moreover, the AuCu3-100 shows positive correlation between the applied potential and CO FE, realizing the CO/H2 ratio from 1:5 up to 6:1. The revealed structureproperty relationship in this work provides new insights into the selectivity descriptors in ECR to syngas, and lays the foundation for the design and synthesis of cost-efficient alloy catalysts with higher selectivity to more complicated ECR products.
